title: Alternate Picking
goal: Pick a clean, even line in A minor across all six strings, and hold it over a band for eight bars.
assumes: You can fret single notes cleanly, you hold a pick, and you can play eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM. No speed is assumed. The minutes listed are one pass through the material; expect to come back to each Step for days or weeks.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM

orderRationale: Time first, then speed of the same motion, then control of it (accents), then one problem at a time across strings. The Beginner Level gives each idea a second Step before strings are crossed: on other strings, in mixed rhythms and in whole tunes. It departs from the starting order in one place: pentatonic patterns come before three notes per string, and bursts follow them. Two notes per string gives the same crossing over and over, so it is the natural first application, while three per string changes crossing type on every string. Bursts come after both so they can use real shapes rather than chromatic fingers. Outside picking is taught before inside because most players find it easier, and both are named so a teacher can overrule that. Up to tempo (added 2026-11-18) sits after the cross-string runs: the Advanced Level otherwise passed no faster than the Intermediate one, and its figures are ones the player already knows, so speed is the only new thing.
gradingLimits: Everything here is graded on timing and notes for single picked notes, which is what the app is built for, and none of it has been tried on a real guitar yet. The faster the line, the less sure the grade. Your setup adds a small delay between playing a note and the app hearing it; up to sixteenths at 100 BPM that makes no difference, and above that, read the evenness score as provisional. Heavy distortion and compression blur where each note starts, so a clean or light-crunch tone is the honest setting for a graded take. Nothing faster than sixteenths at 200 BPM is graded, and no Exercise here goes that far.

steps.title: Even eighths on one string
steps.goal: Down-up, down-up, every note the same length, at the speed of a slow walk.
steps.why: Every later Step is this motion, faster or across strings. If eighths are uneven at 80 BPM, sixteenths at 120 will only hide it for a while. One string means there is only one thing to think about: time.
howTo: Hold the pick between thumb and the side of the first finger, with a little of its tip showing. Move it from the wrist, small, like shaking water off the end of a finger.
Down on the beat, up on the 'and'. The pick stays in the same place above and below the string and travels as little as it can.
Rest the side of the picking hand lightly on the bridge so the low strings stay quiet.
steps.payoff: A tune over an open string that sits on the click from the first Exercise, and a riff that already sounds like a riff.

exercises.title: A tune over the open E
exercises.purpose: A melody in A minor with the open high E sounding between every note, the pedal-tone sound of a baroque prelude or a rock guitar's showpiece, slowed right down. The fretting hand moves once a beat, so nearly all your attention stays on the pick.
howTo: Eighth notes on the high E string, 60 BPM up to a pass at 100. Downstroke on every fretted note, upstroke on every open E: strictly down-up, never two the same way.

The tune is C, B, A, B, then C, D, C, B, then C, B, A, G#, then A, G#, A, B, and round again. First finger on fret 5, third on 7, fourth on 8. Move the hand up two frets for the D at fret 10 in bar 2, and back one fret in bars 3 and 4, so the first finger takes the G# at 4 and the second the A at 5.
Each open E is your time to move the fretting hand. Keep down and up equally loud: uneven pick depth is the usual reason they are not.
exercises.coachLine: Even eighths and the written notes are what I check, after the take. The direction of each stroke is yours to keep: I can't hear it.

cues.say: Count '1 and 2 and' out loud as you play.
Pick each open E like the fretted notes.
Keep the pick on the top string only.
Say the tune's note before you fret it.
Put each fretted note right on the click.
Wait for the click on each fretted note.
Move the fretting hand while the open E rings.
Keep counting '1 and 2 and' to the last note.

exercises.title: Four fingers, one string
exercises.purpose: Bring the fretting hand in without letting it set the time. The fingers land exactly when the pick does.
howTo: First finger on fret 5, one finger per fret. Walk up and back on the A string.
Keep each finger down until the next one lands, and keep the little finger close to the string.
exercises.coachLine: If the notes bunch up, slow down one rung. Timing is what I have to go on here.

cues.say: Land each finger exactly as the pick strikes.
Press each finger right behind the fret.
Keep each finger down until the next lands.
Put each beat's note right on the click.
Wait for the click on each beat's note.
Keep the walk down as even as the walk up.

exercises.title: A minor up one string
exercises.purpose: A melody played by moving the whole hand along the G string, so shifts stop being an event.
howTo: Play the notes of A minor along the G string: frets 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 12 and 14, then back down. Use the first two fingers only and slide the hand between notes. Lift just enough to move.
Sing the notes if you can. A wrong note here is obvious to the ear.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I can say whether the notes were the written ones, and how even they were.

cues.say: Count '1 and 2 and' while the hand moves.
Press each finger down fully before the pick.
Lift the old finger as the new one lands.
Sing each note before you play it.
Arrive at each fret before the click.
Wait for the click before each move.
Move the hand as soon as each note is picked.
Keep the way down as even as the way up.

exercises.title: The low E riff
exercises.purpose: The audible payoff: a palm-muted riff in E. Alternate strokes on a low string feel different, and this is where it counts.
howTo: Rest the side of your palm on the low E, just in front of the bridge, so the open string thuds and still has a pitch.
Strictly down-up, even on the repeated open notes. Rock players often use all downstrokes here; this Exercise is deliberately not that.
exercises.coachLine: I can time the riff and check its notes after the take. Whether the palm mute sounds right is your ear's job.

cues.say: Keep the pick going down-up on every note.
Rest the palm lightly, just by the bridge.
Keep the pick on the low E only.
Press each fretted note fully down.
Put fret 3 and fret 5 right on the click.
Wait for the click on every fretted note.
Pick each open E with the same stroke.
Count the last four notes out loud.

steps.title: Every string, one at a time
steps.goal: The same even eighths on the D, A and B strings, each with a tune of its own.
steps.why: Each string answers the pick differently. The D and A strings are wound and thicker, so the pick meets more of them; the B string is thin and gives way. All three have a neighbour on each side, so a stroke that swings wide hits the wrong string. The first Step played its tunes on the high E, the G and the low E, and only a finger walk on the A string; these are the strings in between. Finding each one by feel now, at a tempo you already hold, leaves only the pick's move to learn when lines start to cross strings.
howTo: Nothing changes in the strokes: down on the beat, up on the 'and'. Even eighths on one string has the grip and the motion; go back to it if either feels unsure.
Before each Exercise, rest the pick on the string it uses and look away from the picking hand. Let the hand learn where that string is.
On the wound strings let less of the pick's tip go past the string. A deep stroke catches on the winding and comes out late.
Keep the stroke small enough that the strings on either side stay silent.
steps.payoff: Three short tunes on three different strings, and a line that visits three strings in four bars, all at the tempo of your first eighths.

exercises.title: A tune on the D string
exercises.purpose: The D string is wound and sits in the middle of the set, so it feels heavier under the pick and is easy to miss. A slow tune on four notes keeps the fretting hand simple while the pick learns the string.
howTo: Eighth notes on the D string, 60 BPM up to a pass at 100. Down on the beat, up on the 'and'.
The notes are the open D, A at fret 7, B at fret 9 and C at fret 10. First finger on fret 7, third on fret 9, fourth on fret 10, and the hand stays where it is.
Bars 1 and 3 are the same: the open D, then A, B, C, B, A, B, C. Bar 2 answers B, A, B, C and holds B for two beats. Bar 4 answers C, B, A, B and holds A for two beats.
Each long note is a downstroke. Count its two beats, and start the next bar with a downstroke too.
exercises.coachLine: Even eighths and the written notes are checked after the take. The direction of each stroke is yours to keep: it cannot be heard.

cues.say: Down on the beat, up on the 'and'.
Pick the D string a little deeper.
Keep the pick on the D string only.
Say A, B, C as you fret them.
Put the open D right on the click.
Wait for the click before the open D.
Count the long note's two beats, then go.
Keep the open D as firm as the fretted notes.
Hold the last A for both beats.

exercises.title: A tune on the A string
exercises.purpose: The A string is thicker again, and the low E beside it is the string a wide stroke hits. The tune sits on frets 5 to 8 and keeps dropping to the open A, so the pick has to stay on its string while the fretting hand comes and goes.
howTo: Eighth notes on the A string, 60 BPM up to a pass at 100.
The notes are the open A, D at fret 5, E at fret 7 and F at fret 8. First finger on fret 5, third on fret 7, fourth on fret 8.

Bar 1 is the open A, then E, F, E, D, E, F, E. Bar 2 is D, E, D, the open A, and a D held for two beats. Bar 3 is F, E, D, E, F, E, D and the open A. Bar 4 is D, F, E, D and the open A held for two beats.
Rest the side of the picking hand on the bridge, over the low E, so that string stays quiet.
exercises.coachLine: Even eighths and the written notes are checked after the take. A stroke that lands on the low E can count as an extra note. A low E ringing under the tune is not checked: listen for it.

cues.say: Count '1 and 2 and' out loud as you play.
Pick the A string a little deeper.
Keep the pick on the A string only.
Say D, E, F as you fret them.
Put the open A right where you count it.
Wait for its count before each open A.
Count the long note's two beats, then go.
Have the next finger ready as the open A rings.
Hold the last open A for both beats.

exercises.title: A tune on the B string
exercises.purpose: The B string is thin, with a string close on each side of it. This tune goes between the open string and frets 5 to 8, so the pick has to stay on one thin string while the fretting hand comes and goes.
howTo: Eighth notes on the B string, 60 BPM up to a pass at 100.
The notes are the open B, E at fret 5, F at fret 6 and G at fret 8. First finger on fret 5, second on fret 6, fourth on fret 8.

Bar 1 is the open B, then E, F, E, the open B again, then E, G, F. Bar 2 is E, F, G, F and a G held for two beats. Bar 3 walks down in pairs and back up: G, G, F, F, E, E, F, G. Bar 4 is G, F, E, the open B, and an E held for two beats.
Keep the first finger just above fret 5 while the open B sounds, so it lands on time.
exercises.coachLine: Even eighths and the written notes are checked after the take. The open Bs are where the time tends to move.

cues.say: Count '1 and 2 and' out loud as you play.
Pick the B string a little deeper.
Keep the pick on the B string only.
Say E, F, G as you fret them.
Put the open B right where you count it.
Wait for its count before each open B.
Count the long note's two beats, then go.
Hover the first finger over fret 5.
Hold the last E for both beats.

exercises.title: A new string at each bar line
exercises.purpose: One string for a whole bar, then another. Every bar ends on a note a full beat long, and the pick moves to the new string while it rings. This is not string crossing yet: in a crossing the pick changes string between two quick notes, and that is the work of the Intermediate Level.
howTo: Six eighth notes and a quarter note in every bar, 60 BPM up to a pass at 100.

Bar 1 is on the A string: A, B, C, B, A, B, then C for a full beat (frets 0, 2, 3, 2, 0, 2, 3). Bar 2 is the same frets on the D string: D, E, F, E, D, E, F. Bar 3 is on the G string, where the top note is at fret 4: G, A, B, A, G, A, B. Bar 4 goes back to the D string: F, E, D, E, F, D, then E for a full beat (frets 3, 2, 0, 2, 3, 0, 2).
First finger on fret 2, second on fret 3, and the third on fret 4 for the B on the G string. The fretting hand never moves along the neck.
While the quarter note rings, move the pick to the next string and rest it there. The first note of every bar is a downstroke.
As the next bar starts, relax the finger on the long note without leaving the string, so it stops and two strings do not ring together.
exercises.coachLine: Even time and the written notes are checked after the take. The move between strings has a whole beat: use all of it.

cues.say: Move to the next string during the long note.
Pick the first note of each bar firmly.
Lift off cleanly when the new string starts.
Say each bar's first note before it comes.
Put each bar's first note right on the click.
Stay on the long note until the next beat.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Keep the open notes as firm as the rest.
Land the pick on the new string, then play.
Count the last bar out loud, on the D string.

steps.difficultyException: The same rate as the Step before, on purpose, and the tunes end their phrases on long notes. What is new is the string under the pick, which the note-rate metric cannot count.

steps.title: Even sixteenths on one string
steps.goal: The same motion at twice the rate, without the hand tightening to get there.
steps.why: Sixteenths are where picking stops being counting and starts being a motion you trust. Doubling the rate exposes any stroke that was bigger than it needed to be, and it is the first place a click and a hand really disagree.
howTo: Make the stroke smaller, not harder. If you feel your forearm lock, slow down one rung: the locked arm is usually what makes the wall.
Count '1 e and a'. Down on 1 and 'and', up on 'e' and 'a'.
Tilt the pick slightly so its edge slides off the string rather than digging in.
steps.payoff: A run of sixteenths you can hold for a full loop, and a melody that sounds busy without feeling frantic.

exercises.title: Change gear, same tune
exercises.purpose: The open-E tune from the first Step, then the same notes twice as fast. Going from eighths to sixteenths without a stumble is the real skill, because every line changes rate.
howTo: Bar 1 is eighths: C, B, A, B with the open E between each. Bar 2 is sixteenths: the first two bars of the open-E tune, C, B, A, B, C, D, C, B, squeezed into one. 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
Down on every fretted note, up on every open E, in both bars. The stroke gets smaller in bar 2, not harder; the pick never skips.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even each half was, and check the notes after the take. The join between the bars is usually where it slips.

cues.say: Make the stroke smaller for the fast half.
Keep the pick moving: never skip a stroke.
Keep the pick on the top string only.
Fret each note before its stroke arrives.
Land the first fast note right on the click.
Play the eighths on the click, no earlier.
Keep every open E as firm as the fretted ones.
Count '1 e and a' through the fast half.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Four fingers at sixteenths
exercises.purpose: The hands have to agree at a rate where they can no longer be managed one note at a time.
howTo: The same four-finger walk as in the first Step, at sixteenths. If the fingers land ahead of the pick, each note sounds twice: a soft tap from the finger, then the picked note. Make the fingers lazier.
exercises.coachLine: Evenness is the number to watch on this one.

cues.say: Let each finger land as the pick strikes.
Keep each finger pressed for its whole note.
Lift the old finger as the new one lands.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

notPooled.reason: The frets get wider toward the nut, so a low position is harder than a high one.

exercises.title: Four of each
exercises.purpose: A melody where the fretting hand moves once a beat and the pick never stops: the rate in the right hand, the music in the left.
howTo: Four sixteenths per note on the top string. Move the left hand exactly on the beat, not a hair before.
This is the tremolo idea in slow motion, and it is a good warm-up on any day.
exercises.coachLine: Four notes per pitch makes the time easy to judge, and I'll check the notes after the take.

cues.say: Count '1 e and a' and change on the 1.
Keep the pick going through all four.
Lift the old finger as the new one lands.
Look at the next fret before the beat.
Change note right on the click.
Change note on the beat, not a hair before.
Have the next fret ready before the beat.
Count '1 e and a' right to the end.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Sixteenth melody on the B string
exercises.purpose: A real line in A minor on one string: if this one sings, your sixteenths are musical rather than merely fast.
howTo: Stay on the B string. Beat 1 uses frets 6, 8 and 10 with the first, second and little fingers: a wider reach than one finger per fret, so open the hand from the first finger. Beat 2 starts with the first finger one fret lower, at fret 5, and it slides back up to fret 6 for the next note. For beat 3 move the whole hand up two frets, so the same fingers take frets 8, 10 and 12, and come back down for beat 4.
Let the first note of each beat be a touch stronger so you can hear where you are.
exercises.coachLine: When this is even and on the written notes, the next Step is ready for you.

cues.say: Count '1 e and a' and keep every note even.
Keep each finger down for its whole note.
Keep the pick on the B string only.
Have the first finger ready on fret 5.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Move the hand with the notes, not after.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: Eighths and sixteenths in one bar
steps.goal: Play a long note and two short ones on one beat, either way round, with the hand moving the same way throughout.
steps.why: Real lines are rarely all one note length. When an eighth and two sixteenths share a beat, the picking hand does not stop for the long note: it keeps its sixteenth motion, and one stroke passes over the string without touching it. Every downstroke stays on a beat or an 'and', where it already was, so the hand itself keeps the time.
howTo: Count '1 e and a' as in Even sixteenths on one string. The hand goes down on 1 and 'and', up on 'e' and 'a', whether or not there is a note there.
A stroke with no note is the same stroke, a little further from the string. Do not stop the hand and start it again.
So every note on a beat or on an 'and' is a downstroke, and every note on an 'e' or an 'a' is an upstroke.
The tab shows no stroke marks in this Step, because some strokes have no note. The rule gives you every one.
To learn a rhythm, lay the fretting hand across the strings so they only click, pick the rhythm alone, then add the notes.
steps.payoff: A long-short-short rhythm, its mirror image, and a melody that changes note length from beat to beat while the hand keeps doing one thing.

exercises.title: Long, short, short
exercises.purpose: An eighth and two sixteenths on every beat. The hand makes four strokes a beat, and the second one, an upstroke, misses the string on purpose.
howTo: An eighth then two sixteenths on every beat, on the G string, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Count '1, and a, 2, and a'.
The strokes you hear are down, down, up: down on the beat, a silent up, down on the 'and', up on the 'a'.
Bar 1 is A at fret 2 on every beat, with the first finger. Bar 2 changes note on each beat: B at fret 4 with the third finger, A at fret 2, B at fret 4, then the open G.
exercises.coachLine: Timing is what is checked, and the usual fault is rushing the two short notes. Which stroke plays which note cannot be heard, so that rule is yours to keep.

cues.say: Count '1, and a' and keep the hand swinging.
Pick the two short notes as firmly as the long.
Let the second stroke pass over the string.
Put the long note right on the click.
Hold the long note until the 'and'.
Keep the open G on time with the rest.
Keep the hand moving up to the last note.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Short, short, long
exercises.purpose: The mirror image: two sixteenths, then an eighth. Now the stroke that misses is the last upstroke of the beat, just before the next beat's downstroke.
howTo: Two sixteenths then an eighth on every beat, on the G string, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Count '1 e and, 2 e and'.
The strokes you hear are down, up, down: down on the beat, up on the 'e', down on the 'and', then a silent up.
Bar 1 is B at fret 4 on every beat, with the third finger. Bar 2 changes note on each beat: the open G, A at fret 2 with the first finger, B at fret 4, then A at fret 2.
exercises.coachLine: Timing is what is checked. The eighth at the end of each beat is the one to wait for: the next beat tends to arrive early. Which stroke plays which note cannot be heard, so that rule is yours to keep.

cues.say: Count '1 e and' and land the eighth on 'and'.
Pick both short notes right through.
Let the last upstroke clear the string.
Put the first short note on the click.
Give the eighth its full length.
Keep the open G on time with the rest.
Keep the hand moving up to the last note.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Both in one bar
exercises.purpose: The two rhythms take turns inside one bar. Where they meet, four sixteenths run together and then two eighths do, so the hand has to hit, miss and hit again without a pause.
howTo: Beats 1 and 3 are an eighth and two sixteenths; beats 2 and 4 are two sixteenths and an eighth. On the G string, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Count '1, and a, 2 e and, 3, and a, 4 e and'.
It comes out as four sixteenths in a row, then two eighths in a row. The two eighths are both downstrokes, because the hand passes over the string between them.
Bar 1 is B at fret 4 throughout, with the third finger. Bar 2 changes note on each beat: A at fret 2 with the first finger, B at fret 4, A at fret 2, then the open G.
exercises.coachLine: Timing is what is checked. If the two eighths come out down, up, the hand has stopped its sixteenth motion: go down a rung and count out loud.

cues.say: Count '1, and a, 2 e and' out loud.
Keep the hand moving on the silent strokes.
Keep the hand moving between the two eighths.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Let the two eighths take their full time.
Keep the open G on time with the rest.
Keep the hand moving up to the last note.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: A melody in both rhythms
exercises.purpose: A melody on the top string whose note lengths change from beat to beat. The fretting hand now moves inside each rhythm, and the picking hand still does its one thing.
howTo: Eighths and sixteenths, with a quarter note to end bars 2 and 4, on the high E string, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
The notes are the open E, A at fret 5, B at fret 7 and C at fret 8, with the first, third and fourth fingers: the frets the open-E tune of the first Step starts on.
Bars 1 and 3 are the same. Long, short, short twice: E, A, B, then C, B, A. Short, short, long: B, C, B. Then two eighths, A and the open E.

Bar 2 is long, short, short twice (C, B, A, then B, A, B), short, short, long (C, B, A) and B for a full beat. Bar 4 is long, short, short (C, B, A), short, short, long (B, C, B), two eighths (A, B) and A for a full beat.
Every note on a beat or an 'and' is a downstroke, the two eighths in a row included.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and time after the take. Stroke direction is not checked: keep the hand swinging in sixteenths and the strokes fall where they should.

cues.say: Keep the hand swinging in sixteenths.
Pick the short notes as firmly as the long.
Keep the pick on the top string only.
Say A, B, C as you fret them.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Count the 'and' before the sixteenths start.
Count the quarter note's beat, then come in.
Keep the open E on time with the rest.
Hold the last A for its full beat.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.difficultyException: Fewer notes to the beat than the Step before, on purpose. The work is the stroke that misses the string, and the note-rate metric counts only notes.

steps.title: Accents where you want them
steps.goal: Put a louder note on any sixteenth you choose, including the ones on an upstroke, without the time moving.
steps.why: Accents prove the picking hand is under control rather than running on its own, and they are what makes a fast line sound like rhythm. An accent on an upstroke is the honest test: most players can only accent downstrokes until they practise this.
howTo: An accent comes from a little more depth and speed in that one stroke. Don't squeeze, and don't let the next note get swallowed.
Keep the unaccented notes quiet on purpose. The contrast is what makes an accent, more than the loud note does.
Use a clean or light-crunch tone. Compression and high gain flatten the difference, for your ear and for the app.
steps.payoff: The same run of notes that used to sound like a typewriter now has a groove in it.

exercises.title: Accent every beat
exercises.purpose: The easy case first: the accent falls on a downstroke, and every beat is marked.
howTo: Accent the first note of each group of four. If everything gets louder, your unaccented notes have crept up.
exercises.coachLine: Accent checks are rough: I can only tell louder from not louder.

cues.say: Count '1 e and a' and accent only the 1.
Play every quiet note, just lighter.
Keep the pick on the A string only.
Put the accent right on the click.
Wait for the click before each accent.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.
Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: Walk the accent
exercises.purpose: One note, four bars, and the accent moves from the first sixteenth to the last. Bars 2 and 4 are accents on upstrokes.
howTo: Same note throughout. Change which note of the four is loud at each bar line, and keep the time dead still while you do.
exercises.coachLine: Bars 2 and 4 are the test. The accent readout is rough, so trust your ear too.

cues.say: Say which note is loud before each bar.
Play every quiet note, just lighter.
Keep the pick on the G string only.
Keep the pulse steady as the accent moves.
Let the accent move, never the beat.
Keep the last accent as steady as the first.

notes: Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: Threes across fours
exercises.purpose: Accents every three sixteenths turn a straight line into a pattern that pulls against the beat: this is the payoff of the Step.
howTo: Accents fall at 3, 3, 3, 3, 4 sixteenths. Tap your foot on the beat, not on the accents, and let the two disagree.
exercises.coachLine: Your accents should fall against the click here, which makes this a good one to listen back to.

cues.say: Tap your foot on the beat, not the accents.
Play every quiet note, just lighter.
Keep the pick on the D string only.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Hold the pulse; let the accents fall.
Have the little finger ready for fret 10.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.
Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: A melody on the accents
exercises.purpose: Fretted accents over an open-string pedal: the tune is only in the loud notes, and you are the one making it come out.
howTo: Between accents the open E keeps going, quietly. Move the fretting hand during the open notes so the accented note is there in time.
exercises.coachLine: If the melody jumps out when you listen back, the Exercise has done its job. I can only check that the accents were louder.

cues.say: Move the fretting hand during the open notes.
Pick every open E, just lightly.
Keep the pick on the top string only.
Have each fretted note ready before its beat.
Wait for the click on every accent.
Let each open E ring until the next accent.
Keep the last accents on the beat.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.
Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

steps.title: Tunes on one string
steps.goal: Play two eight-bar tunes in E minor, one in eighths and sixteenths and one with accents, and play the first with a band.
steps.why: Until now each idea had Exercises to itself: even eighths, even sixteenths, the two in one bar, accents. Music uses them together and goes on for longer than four bars. Eight bars on one string is long enough to lose your place in and short enough to hold in your head, and it is the last thing to settle before the pick has to change strings.
howTo: The tunes are in E minor. On the B string they use the open string and frets 5, 7 and 8; on the high E string, the open string and frets 7, 8 and 10.
The hand keeps the sixteenth motion of Eighths and sixteenths in one bar all the way through: every note on a beat or an 'and' is a downstroke. No strokes are printed here either.
Learn a tune two bars at a time before you play all eight. If you lose your place, come in again at the next bar line.
For the Exercise with a band, use headphones or plug the guitar straight in for a graded take: the band reaching a microphone is something the app has not been tested against.
steps.payoff: Two tunes you can play from start to finish, one of them with a band behind you.

exercises.title: Eight bars in E minor
exercises.purpose: Eight bars in E minor on the B string, with every rhythm of the last Steps in it. It is long enough that you have to know where you are, and that is the new thing.
howTo: Eighths and sixteenths with a long note to end each bar, on the B string, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

The notes are the open B, E at fret 5, F# at fret 7 and G at fret 8. First finger on fret 5, third on fret 7, fourth on fret 8, and the hand stays there. The new note is F#: fret 7 with the third finger, where A tune on the B string had F at fret 6 with the second.

Bars 1, 3, 5 and 7 share one rhythm: long, short, short twice, two eighths, then a note for a full beat. Bars 2, 4 and 6 turn the first two beats round: short, short, long twice, two eighths, a full beat.
Bars 5 and 6 repeat bars 1 and 2. Bar 8 is the ending: four sixteenths, G, F#, E, F#, then two eighths, G and F#, and E for two beats.
The bars start on E, G, G, F#, then E, G, F#, G. The open B comes once in each of bars 2, 4, 6 and 7.
Every note on a beat or an 'and' is a downstroke.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and time after the take, over all eight bars. If one bar keeps slipping, practise that bar alone at a slower rung and come back.

cues.say: Count each bar's number as it starts.
Pick the short notes as firmly as the long.
Keep the pick on the B string only.
Say each bar's first note before it comes.
Put each bar's first note on the click.
Stay on the long note until the next beat.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Keep the open B on time with the rest.
Hold the last E for both beats.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Accents on the beat, then on the 'and'
exercises.purpose: One melody, played twice. The first time each melody note is on the beat, long and accented. The second time it is the long note at the end of the beat, so the accent lands on the 'and'. Between the melody notes the open E stays quiet.
howTo: Eighths and sixteenths with accents, on the high E string, 50 BPM up to a pass at 75.
The melody is on frets 7, 8 and 10: B, C and D, with the first, second and fourth fingers. Every other note is the open E.
Bars 1 to 4: an accented melody note, then two quiet open Es, on every beat. The melody is B, D, C, B, then D, C, B, C, then D, B, C, D, then C, D and a B held for two beats.
Bars 5 to 8: the same melody with each beat turned round: two quiet open Es, then the accented note on the 'and'. The last B falls on beat 3 of bar 8 and is held for two beats.
Every accent is a downstroke. Play the open Es lightly: the contrast is what makes the accent, as in Accents where you want them.
exercises.coachLine: Timing, and whether the accented notes were louder than the rest, after the take. The accent check is rough: louder or not louder is all it can tell. The notes themselves are not checked here.

cues.say: Play the open Es lightly; lean on the tune.
Pick every open E, just lightly.
Keep the pick on the top string only.
Put each accent right on its beat or 'and'.
Second time through, wait for the 'and'.
Count the held B's two beats, then go on.
Let each open E ring until the next note.
Hold the last B for both beats.

notes: Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: Eight bars in E minor, with a band
exercises.purpose: Eight bars in E minor again, note for note, with drums and bass under it. You know the notes, so the band is the only new thing: there is more to listen to than a click, and the tune has to keep its place inside it.
howTo: The eight bars of Eight bars in E minor, unchanged: eighths and sixteenths on the B string, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

The bass follows one chord a bar: E minor, C, G, D, then E minor, C, D and E minor. The first note and the long last note of every bar are notes of that bar's chord, so each bar should sound like arriving and staying.
Listen to the snare drum, not to your own fingers. If you get lost, wait for the next bar line and come in there.
Use headphones or plug the guitar straight in for a graded take: the band reaching a microphone is something the app has not been tested against.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take; staying with the band for all eight bars is the whole job.

cues.say: Listen to the snare drum, not your fingers.
Pick the short notes as firmly as the long.
Keep the pick on the B string only.
Say each bar's first note before it comes.
Land each bar's first note with the band.
Stay on the long note until the next beat.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Keep the open B on time with the band.
If you get lost, come in at the next bar.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

backing.chart: Em | C | G | D | Em | C | D | Em

steps.difficultyException: The tunes mix long and short notes, so they have fewer notes a second than the Step before. What is new is eight bars in a row and three ideas held together, which the note-rate metric cannot count.

steps.title: Crossing two strings
steps.goal: Change strings with no gap and no scrape, on both kinds of crossing.
steps.why: This is where alternate picking actually gets hard. On one string the pick has nothing in its way; between two strings it has to get over one of them. There are only two kinds of crossing, and every line in the rest of this Path is built from them.
howTo: Outside: a downstroke on the lower-pitched string, then an upstroke on the higher one. Each stroke starts from outside the pair, so the pick travels around the strings.
Inside: an upstroke on the lower-pitched string, then a downstroke on the higher one. Each stroke starts between the two strings, so the pick must hop out of the gap.
Let the pick clear the strings by as little as you can. Much of this motion comes from a small tilt of the wrist, so try it slowly with no click first.
steps.payoff: A short A minor lick that used to trip every time now rolls, and you can name which crossing is the one that catches you.

exercises.title: Outside, two notes
exercises.purpose: One outside crossing, over and over, with nothing else to think about.
howTo: Down on the G string, up on the B string, slowly. Your pick travels around the outside of the pair.
exercises.coachLine: I can time these and hear if notes go missing. Which way the pick went is up to you to keep honest.

cues.say: Go around the outside of the two strings.
Pick the B string as firmly as the G string.
Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
Put the G string note right on the click.
Wait for the click before each G string note.
Keep the pick close as you cross.

exercises.title: Inside, two notes
exercises.purpose: The same two notes, starting from the top string so that the pick is trapped between them. Most players feel the difference at once.
howTo: Down on the B string, up on the G string. The pick works inside the gap and has to escape at each change.
exercises.coachLine: If this one is uneven and the last one was not, that is useful to know. Stay at the tempo that stays even.

cues.say: Start down on the B string; keep it even.
Pick the G string as firmly as the B string.
Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
Put the B string note right on the click.
Wait for the click on the B string.
Make the hop smaller, not faster.

exercises.title: Outside, moving notes
exercises.purpose: A moving pair at sixteenths, all outside crossings, so the fretting hand gets busier while the pick path stays the same.
howTo: Sixteenths on the G and B strings, each pair twice: C and E, D and G, C and F, D and E. First finger on the frets at 5, third finger on the G string's 7, second on the B string's 6, little finger on its 8.
The strokes never change: down on the G string, up on the B string. Only the fretting hand has anything new to do.
exercises.coachLine: Evenness plus the right notes, after the take.

cues.say: Keep the strokes the same; only frets change.
Pick the B string as firmly as the G string.
Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
Have the next finger ready before each pair.
Put each new pair right on the beat.
Wait for the click before each new pair.
Keep the pick close as you cross.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Inside, moving notes
exercises.purpose: The same four pairs, top note first, all inside crossings, so you can compare the two honestly.
howTo: The same four pairs in sixteenths with the B string first: E and C, G and D, F and C, E and D, each twice.
Down on the B string, up on the G string. If you hear a tiny gap at each change, that is the pick hopping out from between the strings. Make the hop smaller, not faster.
exercises.coachLine: Compare this take with the outside one. The gap between them is what you are working on.

cues.say: Keep the pick path the same; only frets change.
Pick the G string as firmly as the B string.
Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
Have the next finger ready before each pair.
Put each new pair right on the beat.
Wait for the click before each new pair.
Make the hop smaller, not faster.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: An all-outside A minor lick
exercises.purpose: Eight notes that sound like a real lick and happen to contain only outside crossings. This is the Step's payoff.
howTo: Start on a downstroke on the D string. Every string change works out as outside; keep that going by never adding a stroke.
exercises.coachLine: This is music now. Get it even, then speed it up one rung at a time.

cues.say: Start down, and never add a stroke.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the strings in use.
Say the lick's first note before you start.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Keep the pick close as you cross.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: Pentatonic patterns
steps.goal: Play the A minor pentatonic box in the sequences you actually hear in rock and blues solos.
steps.why: Two notes per string means a crossing every other note, and the same kind of crossing each time. That is exactly what makes pentatonic runs harder to pick than they look, and it is why they come right after crossings. You get a sound you already recognise as your reward.
howTo: Box 1 of A minor pentatonic sits at fret 5, two notes on every string. The first finger plays fret 5 on all six strings. The other note is fret 8 with the little finger on the low E, B and top strings, and fret 7 with the third finger on the A, D and G strings.
Blues and Pentatonics teaches the box slowly over a band in its first Step.

Starting on a downstroke on the first note of a string, every change going up is inside. Coming down from a downstroke on the first note of a string, every change is outside. Where the stroke falls decides it, so you can choose.
Roll a fingertip across when two notes share a fret on neighbouring strings, rather than lifting and placing it.
Count '1-trip-let, 2-trip-let'. Three even notes a click, with the first one on it.

Three of the Exercises here are in triplets. Keep the strokes strictly down-up, so beats 2 and 4 start on an upstroke. That is correct. Do not add a stroke to fix it. Rhythm Foundations drills triplets on their own in its Intermediate Level, in the Step 'Three to a beat'.
steps.payoff: The run from a hundred solos you have heard, at a tempo where it is clean, and the same lick working in three keys.

exercises.title: The box, up and down
exercises.purpose: The whole box in plain triplets, so the map and the crossings settle together.
howTo: Six strings up and back. The turn on the top string lands the next downstroke on the box's lower fret, so the descent is inside crossings too: the whole loop is one kind, and you get a long look at it.
Each Take plays one of the five boxes: the same five notes, further up the neck from box 1 to box 5. Read the frets from the tab.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say whether the notes were the box and how even they were.

cues.say: Count '1-trip-let' and keep the triplets even.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Name the next two notes before you play them.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the held note out, then start again.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the way down as even as the way up.

exercises.title: Inside on two strings of the box
exercises.purpose: Six notes, all inside crossings, isolated from the hardest corner of the pentatonic.
howTo: G and B strings. Start down on the G string. Both crossings are inside, and there is no easy one to rest on.
exercises.coachLine: This is the corner the long runs trip on. Evenness tells the story.

cues.say: Start down on the G string; keep it even.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
Have the little finger ready for fret 8.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Make the hop smaller, not faster.

exercises.title: Descending threes
exercises.purpose: The classic pentatonic run: groups of three coming down the box, each group starting one note lower.
howTo: Triplets, so every group starts on a beat. Three is odd, so each group starts on the opposite stroke from the last one, which is the whole point: the crossings keep changing. Accent the first note of each group a little, as in the Step 'Accents where you want them'. Every second accent is an upstroke.
exercises.coachLine: A long run like this usually slips in the same place. Listening back will show you where.

cues.say: Lean a little on the first of each three.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Start each group one note lower.
Put each group's first note on the click.
Wait for the click before each group.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the low strings as even as the top.

exercises.title: Ascending fours
exercises.purpose: Sixteenths in groups of four climbing the box: harder than threes, because more of the crossings fall on the weak part of the beat.
howTo: Say the group's first note to yourself. It lands on every beat, so if you lose it you have lost the sequence.
exercises.coachLine: Stay on a rung that keeps it even. Fast and rough teaches the wrong thing here.

cues.say: Count the first note of each four on the beat.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Start each group one note higher.
Put each group's first note on the click.
Wait for the click before each group.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the top strings as even as the low.

exercises.title: One lick, three keys
exercises.purpose: Your all-outside lick moved through A, D and E minor pentatonic, so the shape stops being tied to fret 5.
howTo: Two bars at fret 5, one at fret 10, one at fret 12. Shift during the last note of the bar. The strokes do not change.
exercises.coachLine: The shift is the risk. If a note goes missing, look at the bar line first.

cues.say: Keep the strokes the same in every key.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the strings in use.
Look at the new fret before you shift.
Arrive at the new fret before the click.
Wait for the click after each shift.
Shift during each bar's last note.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Hold the shape as you move up the neck.

steps.difficultyException: The rate drops because the lines get long: six strings of crossings with no repeat to lean on, which a per-note metric does not count.

steps.title: Three notes per string
steps.goal: Run the A minor scale in three-per-string shapes, where the crossing type changes on every string.
steps.why: An odd number of notes per string flips the stroke at each change, so outside and inside crossings take turns. This is the shape of most fast scalar playing, and it gives you a long scale without a position shift to manage.
howTo: Each string has three notes, fretted with first, second and little fingers or first, third and little fingers, depending on the gaps. Open the hand from the first finger; don't twist the wrist to reach.
Keep the thumb relaxed behind the neck. It should not be squeezing against your fingers.
Ascending, the changes alternate outside then inside. Say which one is next until you stop needing to.
steps.payoff: A two-octave A minor run, and a six-note lick you will use for the rest of your life.

exercises.title: The six-note lick, descending
exercises.purpose: A classic six-note cell on the top two strings in which both crossings are inside. It is a real lick, not a drill.
howTo: C, B, A on the top string, then G, F, E on the B string, all in triplets. Start on a downstroke, and it stays down on each repeat.
exercises.coachLine: Even triplets first. This one is worth owning at a slow tempo before it gets fast.

cues.say: Count '1-trip-let' and keep it even.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
Say the six notes once before you start.
Put each group's first note on the click.
Wait for the click before each group.
Make the hop smaller, not faster.

variants.label: B minor
howTo: D, C#, B on the top string, then A, G, F# on the B string, all in triplets. Start on a downstroke, and it stays down on each repeat.

variants.label: C minor
howTo: Eb, D, C on the top string, then Bb, Ab, G on the B string, all in triplets. Start on a downstroke, and it stays down on each repeat.

variants.label: D minor
howTo: F, E, D on the top string, then C, Bb, A on the B string, all in triplets. Start on a downstroke, and it stays down on each repeat.

variants.label: E minor
howTo: G, F#, E on the top string, then D, C, B on the B string, all in triplets. Start on a downstroke, and it stays down on each repeat.

variants.label: G minor
howTo: Bb, A, G on the top string, then F, Eb, D on the B string, all in triplets. Start on a downstroke, and it stays down on each repeat.

exercises.title: The six-note lick, ascending
exercises.purpose: The mirror image, in which both crossings are outside, so the two versions tell you which hop you own.
howTo: Triplets. In A minor: E, F, G on the B string (frets 5, 6, 8), then A, B, C on the top string (5, 7, 8), twice. Fingers 1, 2 and 4, then 1, 3 and 4.
Start on a downstroke. The B string ends on a downstroke and the top string starts on an upstroke, so the pick travels around the outside of the pair at each change.
exercises.coachLine: Compare this with the descending take. A big difference is worth a note in your practice.

cues.say: Cross the strings on the outside each time.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
Say the six notes once before you start.
Put each group's first note on the click.
Wait for the click before each group.
Keep the pick close as you cross.

variants.label: B minor
howTo: Triplets. In B minor: F#, G, A on the B string (frets 7, 8, 10), then B, C#, D on the top string (7, 9, 10), twice. Fingers 1, 2 and 4, then 1, 3 and 4.
Start on a downstroke. The B string ends on a downstroke and the top string starts on an upstroke, so the pick travels around the outside of the pair at each change.

variants.label: C minor
howTo: Triplets. In C minor: G, Ab, Bb on the B string (frets 8, 9, 11), then C, D, Eb on the top string (8, 10, 11), twice. Fingers 1, 2 and 4, then 1, 3 and 4.
Start on a downstroke. The B string ends on a downstroke and the top string starts on an upstroke, so the pick travels around the outside of the pair at each change.

variants.label: D minor
howTo: Triplets. In D minor: A, Bb, C on the B string (frets 10, 11, 13), then D, E, F on the top string (10, 12, 13), twice. Fingers 1, 2 and 4, then 1, 3 and 4.
Start on a downstroke. The B string ends on a downstroke and the top string starts on an upstroke, so the pick travels around the outside of the pair at each change.

variants.label: E minor
howTo: Triplets.
Start on a downstroke. The B string ends on a downstroke and the top string starts on an upstroke, so the pick travels around the outside of the pair at each change.

variants.label: G minor
howTo: Triplets. In G minor: D, Eb, F on the B string (frets 3, 4, 6), then G, A, Bb on the top string (3, 5, 6), twice. Fingers 1, 2 and 4, then 1, 3 and 4.
Start on a downstroke. The B string ends on a downstroke and the top string starts on an upstroke, so the pick travels around the outside of the pair at each change.

exercises.title: Three strings, up and down
exercises.purpose: Now both kinds of crossing appear in one line, one straight after the other.
howTo: A up to B and back on the bottom three strings. First, third and little fingers on the low two strings. On the D string the little finger stretches a fret further, to fret 9.
exercises.coachLine: When it is even both ways, the whole neck is the same idea with more strings.

cues.say: Count '1 e and a' and keep it even.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Reach all the way to fret 9 on the D string.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Keep the pick close as you cross.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Two and a half octaves
exercises.purpose: The whole shape up and down in triplets, a small hand shift included where the top strings move up a fret.
howTo: The hand moves up one fret when you reach the B string and one more at the top string, and back on the way down. Move during the string change, not after it.
exercises.coachLine: Long lines are where time drifts. Evenness across the whole take is the number.

cues.say: Count '1-trip-let' and keep it even.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Count three notes on each string.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the held note out, then start again.
Shift as you cross to the B string.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the way down as even as the way up.

steps.title: Speed bursts
steps.goal: Play short runs above your clean tempo, and land on time, without tensing up for the whole bar.
steps.why: You can't practise speed by doing everything slowly and you can't do it by flailing. A burst is the honest middle: one beat of real speed, then a rest long enough that the hand lets go. Most players find a burst is several rungs above what they can sustain, and that tells them the wall is stamina or tension rather than how fast the fingers can go.
howTo: Rest between bursts. The rest is half the Exercise: let the hand go soft before the next one.
Aim at the landing note, not at the run. If you land on time, the run was fine.
Stay above your comfortable tempo here, and use the app's ramp to find where bursts stop being clean.
steps.payoff: You will hear yourself play a short run far faster than you thought you could, and it will be clean.

exercises.title: One beat on, one beat off
exercises.purpose: The shortest honest burst: four notes and a landing, twice a bar.
howTo: Four sixteenths up one string, one finger per fret from the first finger, then a quarter note on the third finger. Twice a bar.
Everything relaxes during the quarter note: let the hand go soft before the next burst. Start above the tempo you can hold for a whole bar.
exercises.coachLine: Landing on time counts more than the run. Timing and missed notes are what I have here.

cues.say: Land the long note right with the click.
Pick every note of the burst right through.
Stop each burst cleanly on the long note.
Start each burst right on the click.
Wait for the click before each burst.
Count the long note's beat, then go.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did the last note land with the click, and did the hand let go in the rest?

notPooled.reason: The frets get wider toward the nut, so a low position is harder than a high one.

exercises.title: Two beats on, two off
exercises.purpose: Twice the length with the same rest, so you find out how much of the speed survives eight notes.
howTo: Eight sixteenths, up the four fingers from fret 5 and back, then a half note on fret 7.
The halfway point of the run, where it turns round on the little finger, is where the time usually moves. Aim at the half note and let the run carry you there.
exercises.coachLine: If one beat was clean and two is not, that is a stamina question and not a speed one.

cues.say: Count the burst, then land the half note.
Pick every note of the burst right through.
Stop each burst cleanly on the long note.
Start each burst right on the click.
Wait for the click before each burst.
Count the half note's two beats, then go.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Expanding bursts
exercises.purpose: One beat, then two, three and four beats on, the classic way of walking a burst into a line.
howTo: The bar tells you how long to keep going. Bar 4 has no rest, so the hand has to stay loose while moving.
exercises.coachLine: Most people slip somewhere in the third bar. It helps to know which one is yours.

cues.say: Play one more beat each bar, then rest.
Pick every note of the burst right through.
Stop each burst cleanly on the long note.
Start each burst right on the click.
Wait for the click before each burst.
Count the rest out, then start the burst.
Keep going through the last bar: no rest.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The six-note burst, into a landing
exercises.purpose: The descending six-note lick from the Step 'Three notes per string', all six notes in one beat, then a walk down to A: this is how a fast run actually gets used in a solo.
howTo: Sextuplets are six even notes to one click.
One beat of sextuplets from the top string, then D, C and A as quarter notes. Land exactly on beat 2.
exercises.coachLine: Fast notes on a real rig are the hardest to time, so trust the landing and your own ear as much as the numbers.

cues.say: Land the first quarter note on the click.
Pick every note of the burst right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the strings in use.
Say D, C, A as you walk down.
Start each burst right on the click.
Wait for the click before each burst.
Count the last quarter note, then start.
Keep the pick close as you cross.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: On a recording, can you still hear all six notes as six?

steps.difficultyException: The metric averages over the rests. Inside a burst the local rate is well above any earlier Step, which is the point.

steps.title: Cross-string runs
steps.goal: Keep alternate strokes going over string skips and long lines across all six strings.
steps.why: So far crossings have been a neighbour at a time. Real lines jump a string and cover the whole neck, and they make you aim. This is the Step where the pick stops following your fingers and starts knowing where it is going.
howTo: On a skip, let the pick travel in a small arc over the string in between. Do not lift the whole forearm.
Mute the strings you are not using with the side of the picking hand and with spare fretting fingers. Noise appears on crossings before it appears anywhere else.
Read long lines in groups, not note by note.
steps.payoff: A climbing octave line, a chromatic crawl across all six strings, and an arpeggio line that sounds like a progression on its own.

exercises.title: Octaves across a skipped string
exercises.purpose: Every note is a string skip and the same two fingers do all the fretting, so the aim is all that is left to practise.
howTo: First finger on the A string, third on the G string. Down on the A string, up on the G string, and a small shift between pairs. All of these are outside crossings.
exercises.coachLine: If notes go missing here it is usually the skip or the shift. Slow down until neither is a surprise.

cues.say: Aim the pick at the far string before you go.
Pick the G string note as firmly as the A.
Let the first finger rest on the skipped string.
Keep the same two fingers on every pair.
Put each A string note right on the click.
Wait for the click before each new pair.
Shift right after each pair's second note.
Stay clear of the skipped string.

exercises.title: The chromatic crawl
exercises.purpose: One finger per fret on all six strings, up and back. It is not music, and it is the fastest way to find which crossing or finger is weak.
howTo: Up with 1-2-3-4 on each string and back with 4-3-2-1. Keep each finger down until the next string needs it.
exercises.coachLine: This is a diagnostic, so play it slowly enough to hear the weakest change.

cues.say: Count '1 e and a' and keep it even.
Keep each finger down until the next string.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Say '1-2-3-4' with the fingers on each string.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the way down as even as the way up.

exercises.title: A minor in fours
exercises.purpose: A long scale line in groups of four, up and back on three strings: this is what most fast lines are made of.
howTo: Each group starts one scale note higher. Stay with the beat: the first note of each group lands on it.
exercises.coachLine: The turn around at the top is the place to listen to.

cues.say: Put the first note of each group on the beat.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Start each group one scale note on.
Put each group's first note on the click.
Wait for the click before each group.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the groups coming down even to the end.

exercises.title: Picked arpeggios: Am, F, C, G
exercises.purpose: Four strings, strict alternate strokes, and a chord progression you can hear in the single notes. The hand barely moves and it sounds like a whole band.
howTo: Each bar is one chord, up and down twice. Am to F moves one note. Stay in fifth position.
These are picked, not swept: every stroke alternates even though the notes run across strings.
exercises.coachLine: I'll check the notes against the chords after the take. Whether it rings like a chord or sounds separated is yours to judge.

cues.say: Alternate every stroke, even across strings.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the strings in use.
Know each bar's chord before it comes.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the last chord as even as the first.

variants.label: C minor
howTo: Each bar is one chord, up and down twice. Cm to Ab moves one note. Stay in eighth position.
These are picked, not swept: every stroke alternates even though the notes run across strings.

variants.label: D minor
howTo: Each bar is one chord, up and down twice. Dm to Bb moves one note. Stay in tenth position.
These are picked, not swept: every stroke alternates even though the notes run across strings.

variants.label: G minor
howTo: Each bar is one chord, up and down twice. Gm to Eb moves one note. Stay in third position.
These are picked, not swept: every stroke alternates even though the notes run across strings.

steps.title: Up to tempo
steps.goal: Take the lick, the three-string scale and the six-note pattern you already know up to the tempo real lines are played at.
steps.why: Everything so far was passed at a moderate tempo, where a slightly big stroke still works. Fifteen or twenty clicks higher it doesn't: the motion has to get smaller, not faster, and the crossings you could think about now have to happen by themselves. These are figures you know, so the only new thing is the speed.
howTo: Start two rungs below the tempo you passed the figure at, and listen for the first rung where it stops sounding easy. That rung is today's work; stay on it.
Make the stroke smaller as the tempo rises. If the forearm tightens, drop a rung and find the small stroke again.
Use the bursts from the Speed bursts Step: play one beat at the new tempo and stop, then two beats, before you try the loop.
steps.payoff: The A minor lick at a tempo that sounds fast, and a scale run across all six strings that holds together.

exercises.title: Both licks, faster
exercises.purpose: The all-outside lick for a bar, then its mirror with every crossing inside, for a bar. Side by side at speed, the weaker crossing has nowhere to hide.
howTo: Sixteenths. Bar 1 is the outside lick twice, starting on the D string. Bar 2 stays on the G and B strings, starting on a downstroke on the G string, and every crossing in it is inside.
If one bar is clean and the other is not, practise the other alone for a minute and come back.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even each bar was and check the notes after the take. At this speed evenness is the number to trust.

cues.say: Count '1 e and a' and keep it even.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the strings in use.
Say the lick's first note before you start.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the inside bar as even as the outside.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Three strings, faster
exercises.purpose: The three-notes-per-string run up and back, from three different starting strings, at a tempo where the stretch and the crossings have to be automatic.
howTo: Sixteenths, sixteen notes, strictly down-up. The crossings alternate outside and inside going up.
Keep the fingers close to the strings. At this tempo a finger that lifts high arrives late.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

cues.say: Count '1 e and a' and keep it even.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Have every finger ready before it plays.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Keep the pick close as you cross.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The six-note lick, six to a click
exercises.purpose: C, B, A, G, F, E on the top two strings as sextuplets, round and round. The six-note burst from the Speed bursts Step, now without the rest after it.
howTo: Six notes to the click, starting on a downstroke; the count is even, so every repeat starts down too.
Accent the first note of each beat a little. Without it six fast notes turn into a blur with no beat in it.
exercises.coachLine: Fast notes are the hardest for me to place, so read the evenness as provisional and trust a recording as well.

cues.say: Lean a little on the first of each six.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
Say the six notes once before you start.
Put the first of each six on the click.
Wait for the click before each six.
Make the hop smaller, not faster.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: On a recording, can you still hear all six notes as six?

variants.label: B minor
variants.purpose: D, C#, B, A, G, F# on the top two strings as sextuplets, round and round. The six-note burst from the Speed bursts Step, now without the rest after it.

variants.label: C minor
variants.purpose: Eb, D, C, Bb, Ab, G on the top two strings as sextuplets, round and round. The six-note burst from the Speed bursts Step, now without the rest after it.

variants.label: D minor
variants.purpose: F, E, D, C, Bb, A on the top two strings as sextuplets, round and round. The six-note burst from the Speed bursts Step, now without the rest after it.

variants.label: E minor
variants.purpose: G, F#, E, D, C, B on the top two strings as sextuplets, round and round. The six-note burst from the Speed bursts Step, now without the rest after it.

exercises.title: Two and a half octaves in sixteenths
exercises.purpose: All six strings of A minor, three notes per string, up and back in sixteenths, with a held note to finish. The long run from the Intermediate Level, now in sixteenths.
howTo: The hand moves up one fret at the B string and again at the top string, and back on the way down. Move during the string change.
Read it in strings, not in notes: three, three, three. The beat falls on a different finger each time, so keep the click in your ear.
exercises.coachLine: This is the Step's test piece. I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

cues.say: Keep the click in your ear through the run.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Count three notes on each string.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Shift as you cross to the B string.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Land the last note and hold it.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: The stamina minute
steps.goal: Hold an even line for sixty seconds at a tempo you could play for ten.
steps.why: Speed that lasts four bars is a party trick. Holding a tempo for a minute is what shows you are not playing on tension, because tension is what runs out. It also gives you honest information: the last ten seconds show the real state of your technique.
howTo: Choose a rung about 20% below your clean tempo. It should feel slow for the first ten seconds.
Breathe. If the shoulder comes up, drop it during a bar line without stopping.
Stop at any pain in the hand, wrist or forearm. A tired forearm is one thing and pain is another; pain ends the set.
steps.payoff: A full minute of sixteenths that sounds the same at the end as at the start.

exercises.title: One minute, one string
exercises.purpose: Stamina without any other question: the four-finger walk for a whole minute.
howTo: The sixteenth-note walk, sixty seconds, no stops. If the time slips late in the take, the rung was too high.
exercises.coachLine: If I stop catching notes on a long take, trust that report over your doubts about your hands. Long unbroken playing is something the listening has not been proven on.

cues.say: Start at a tempo you can hold a whole minute.
Pick every note right through to the end.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Keep the stroke as small in the last seconds.

notes: Long unbroken playing, especially high-gain, can drown out where each note starts, so the app may stop hearing you. Unproven either way; if the app says it did not catch enough, believe that before you doubt your hands.

notPooled.reason: The frets get wider toward the nut, so a low position is harder than a high one.

exercises.title: One minute, the box
exercises.purpose: The same minute with crossings in it, which is where stamina really gets used.
howTo: Box 1 of A minor pentatonic at fret 5, all six strings up and back, in triplets, three to the click, for one minute without stopping.
Keep the crossings small: they grow as you tire. If the pick starts catching on the way across, the rung was too high.
exercises.coachLine: Compare the first and last quarter of the take. A drop there is the point of doing this.

cues.say: Keep the crossings small for the whole minute.
Pick every note right through to the end.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the held note out, then start again.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the crossings small right to the end.

notes: Long unbroken playing, especially high-gain, can drown out where each note starts, so the app may stop hearing you. Unproven either way; if the app says it did not catch enough, believe that before you doubt your hands.

exercises.title: One minute, three per string
exercises.purpose: The hardest of the three: three strings of A minor up and back, sixteenths, with both crossing types.
howTo: Sixty seconds. If this one falls apart well before the others did, go back to crossings for a few days, as it is not an endurance problem.
exercises.coachLine: When the box and this one hold up side by side, you are ready for the band.

cues.say: Start at a tempo you can hold a whole minute.
Pick every note right through to the end.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the stroke as small in the last seconds.

notes: Long unbroken playing, especially high-gain, can drown out where each note starts, so the app may stop hearing you. Unproven either way; if the app says it did not catch enough, believe that before you doubt your hands.

steps.difficultyException: The tempo comes down on purpose: this Step is about holding a line for a minute, a demand the note-rate metric does not count.

steps.title: A clean run over the band
steps.goal: Play an eight-bar line over Am, F, C, G with a real band behind you, and stay even when the click is no longer the only thing in your ears.
steps.why: A click forgives nothing and a band hides everything, which is why this is a separate skill. The drums give you a pulse with a feel to it, the bass tells you where the changes are, and your line has to fit between them. This is the reason you did all of the rest.
howTo: Every written line lands on a note of the chord on each bar line. Play it on your own first, with no band, and listen for those notes.
Listen to the snare, not to your own fingers. If you get lost, catch the next bar line and carry on.
Use direct input or headphones for a graded take: the band reaching a microphone is something the app has not been tested against.
steps.payoff: You play a solo-length line over a band and it sounds like you meant it.

exercises.title: The eight-bar line, eighths
exercises.purpose: A composed line at a rate you can certainly play, so the chord changes under it are the only new thing.
howTo: Eighth notes for eight bars: Am, F, C, G, twice round, on the top four strings in fifth position, with the first finger dropping back to fret 4 for the B in bars 4 and 8.
Every bar starts on a note of its chord, so hear the bar lines land. Bar 8 climbs up the B string, and the line starts again from the A on the D string.
exercises.coachLine: Band on, and all I need is that you stay with it. I'll report the notes after the take.

cues.say: Stay with the band; count each bar.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Say each bar's first note before it comes.
Land each bar's first note with the band.
Let the band lead; sit back on the eighths.
Drop the first finger to fret 4 on the G string.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Climb the B string to the last note.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

backing.chart: Am | F | C | G | Am | F | C | G

exercises.title: Four bars, eighths into sixteenths
exercises.purpose: A fill at the end of every bar. Changing gear in time with a band is what makes a line sound like a player, not like a pattern.
howTo: Let the eighths sit back, and let the sixteenths lead into the next bar line, without speeding up.
exercises.coachLine: The fills are what tend to rush. Listening back to one take with the band is often enough to hear it.

cues.say: Let the eighths sit back with the band.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Say each bar's first note before it comes.
Land each bar's first note with the band.
Land the fill's first note on its beat.
Have the first finger ready for the G string.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Let the last fill lead back to the top.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Four bars of sixteenths
exercises.purpose: The whole Path in four bars: the outside lick, a picked arpeggio, a C arpeggio that reaches up, and a scale run home.
howTo: The groove stays on eighths and you sit on twice its rate. Each bar is one of the ideas you have already practised, so it is mostly a matter of joining them.
exercises.coachLine: This is the graded line. Fast notes on a real rig are the hardest for me to place, so I'd trust the evenness and your ear together.

cues.say: Play four notes to every click.
Pick every note right through.
Keep the stroke small as you cross strings.
Know which idea each bar is before it comes.
Land each bar's first note with the band.
Let the band lead; don't push ahead.
Have the first finger ready for the G string.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Run home in the last bar without rushing.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The whole run, your take
exercises.purpose: The eighths, then the sixteenths, as one take. Record it and listen back: this one is for you, and no number decides it.
howTo: Eight bars of the eighth-note line, then four of the sixteenth line, at whatever rung you can play both. Keep the take if you like it.
exercises.coachLine: No score on this one. Listen back, and if you would play it for someone, the Path is done.

cues.say: Stay with the band from first bar to last.

levels.title: Beginner: one string, even
levels.summary: Eighths, sixteenths and accents, one string at a time: every string in turn, both note lengths in one bar, and at the end whole tunes of eight bars, one of them with a band, so that time and control come before crossing strings.

startHereIf: You can fret single notes cleanly and you hold a pick.
You can play eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM, but sixteenths come out uneven.
An accent on an upstroke feels foreign, or you've never tried one.

warmups.title: A melody up one string
warmups.purpose: Eighths up one string in a minor key, climbing a scale step each bar. A different string and key each time, so there's a tune to follow and a reason to move.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Follow the tune and let the hand travel with it.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

cues.say: Start well under your clean tempo.
Pick every note right through.
Put the first note of each bar on the click.
Wait for the click as each bar starts.
Look one note ahead as you climb.
Keep the top of the climb as even as the start.

levels.title: Intermediate: across the strings
levels.summary: Both kinds of crossing, then the two shapes that use them most: the pentatonic box and three notes per string.

startHereIf: You can hold even sixteenths on one string at about 85 BPM.
You can put an accent on any sixteenth, including on an upstroke, without the time moving.
Your line falls apart when it changes string.

warmups.title: A lick around the chords
warmups.purpose: A short pentatonic lick moved through i, iv and v of a minor key, in a different key and with a different lick each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. The hand moves at the bar line, and the strokes don't change.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

cues.say: Start well under your clean tempo.
Pick every note right through.
Be ready before each new bar starts.
Wait for the click after each move.
Look ahead as each new bar starts.
Keep the pick close to the strings.
Keep the last bar as even as the first.

variants.label: E minor, outside lick
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo.

levels.title: Advanced: speed, length and a band
levels.summary: Bursts above your clean tempo, string skips and long lines, the figures you know taken up to tempo, a full minute without letting up, then a composed run over a band.

startHereIf: You can run A minor three notes per string, across three strings, even at sixteenths 80 BPM.
You can name which crossing is your weaker one, outside or inside. The Step 'Crossing two strings' explains both.
Clean is fine at a moderate tempo and you've hit a speed wall, or you've never held a long line over a band.

warmups.title: A scale in two positions
warmups.purpose: Three strings of a minor scale, up and back from two positions on the neck, starting from a different root each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Change position at the bar line. Keep the shift as small as you can.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

cues.say: Start well under your clean tempo.
Pick every note right through.
Arrive at the new position before the click.
Wait for the click after each move.
Shift in one quick, calm move.
Keep the pick close as you cross.
Keep the upper shape as even as the lower.
